screens.title: Publish-Subscribe Pattern
screens.narratorSegment: Publish-subscribe is a messaging model where senders and receivers are decoupled. A publisher posts typed messages to a named topic without knowing who will read them; subscribers register interest in that topic and receive messages as they arrive. In ROS this model is asynchronous and one-to-many: one publisher can feed many subscribers, and subscribers can come and go without changing the publisher code. A concrete example: a laser scanner node publishes sensor_msgs/LaserScan to /laser/scan and a mapping node plus an obstacle detector can both subscribe independently. A common misconception is thinking the ROS Master forwards messages; it does not. The Master only helps nodes discover each other. After discovery each subscriber opens a direct TCP connection to each publisher so messages flow efficiently without the Master in the data path. Why it matters: this makes systems scalable and low-latency when many nodes need the same data. One pitfall to watch for is assuming message delivery is guaranteed; ROS topics are best-effort. Takeaway: design data flows so subscribers tolerate dropped or delayed messages, and choose queue sizes consciously to balance latency and loss. What sensor stream in your system should be best-effort and which needs guaranteed delivery?

keyIdea.title: Publish-subscribe essence
keyIdea.text: Publishers and subscribers are decoupled; the Master manages discovery only. Messages go direct TCP from publisher to subscriber after discovery.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Publish-Subscribe Pattern
Definition

One-to-many asynchronous messaging

Publishers send typed messages to a topic. Subscribers register interest and receive messages as they arrive. Discovery is handled by the Master; message flow is direct afterward.
Concrete example
A laser publishes LaserScan to /laser/scan. Mapping and obstacle detection both subscribe and receive the same scans concurrently.
Common misconception
The Master forwards messages. It does not — it only provides connection info for direct TCP links.
Key Takeaway

Design nodes to tolerate dropped messages and choose queue_size to balance staleness and loss.

Process Flow

Discovery and direct connection

Publisher registers with Master
Publisher announces topic name and type.
Subscriber queries Master
Master returns publisher addresses for that topic.
Direct TCP connections established
Messages flow directly between nodes without the Master in the path.
Subscribers receive messages asynchronously
Multiple subscribers can consume the same stream independently.

screens.title: Topics, Namespaces, and Naming Rules
screens.narratorSegment: A topic is a named bus for exchanging messages. Names look like paths: for example /robot/cmd_vel or /camera/image_raw. The leading slash denotes a global name; names without a leading slash are relative to the node's namespace. This lets you run multiple robots with identical node code by placing each instance in a different namespace such as /robot1 and /robot2. Topic names follow a filesystem-like hierarchy, so /robot1/cmd_vel and /robot2/cmd_vel are distinct. A concrete example: if you launch two teleop nodes under different namespaces, each teleop publishes to its namespace's /cmd_vel and the appropriate robot will receive commands. A common mistake is forgetting the leading slash and being surprised that topics don't match between nodes. Another misconception is thinking topic names are arbitrary strings; they must conform to ROS naming rules and avoid illegal characters. Why it matters: correct naming is essential when wiring a system with many nodes and when reusing code across multiple robots. Takeaway: choose consistent namespaces and be deliberate about global versus relative topic names. Which naming strategy would you use for two identical wheeled robots operating in the same network?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Topics & Namespaces
Definition

Topic name structure

Topic names use a slash-separated path. A leading slash makes a name global. Names without a leading slash are relative and resolved against the node's namespace.
Example
/robot1/cmd_vel and /robot2/cmd_vel are different topics for two identical robots. Namespaces let identical code run without renaming topics by hand.
Common mistake
Omitting the leading slash can make a topic resolve to a different namespace and appear to not exist to other nodes.
Why it matters

Namespaces are essential when scaling to multiple robots or instances. Use them to avoid naming collisions and to organize topics logically.

Quick reference
Global name
/camera/image_raw
Relative name
camera/image within node namespace
Namespace use-case
Launch two robots with namespaces /robot1 and /robot2 to reuse identical nodes without name collisions.

screens.title: ROS Message Types and rosmsg show
screens.narratorSegment: ROS messages are typed data structures defined in. msg files and compiled into language-specific classes. Standard messages include std_msgs/String for plain text, std_msgs/Int64 for integers, geometry_msgs/Twist for velocity commands, and sensor_msgs/Image for camera data. Knowing a message structure is crucial: it tells you which fields to set and what to expect when subscribing. Use rosmsg show followed by the message type to display the fields and nested types. For example, rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist reveals two Vector3 fields named linear and angular, each with x, y, and z components. A concrete example: for a mobile robot on a plane you typically use linear. x for forward speed and angular. z for rotation rate. A common confusion is assuming Twist has only scalar fields; instead it nests Vector3 structures. Why it matters: choosing the right message type avoids unnecessary conversions and ensures interoperability between nodes. Try rosmsg show on sensor_msgs/LaserScan to see how ranges and angle metadata are organized. Takeaway: always inspect message definitions before publishing or subscribing so you set and read the correct fields. ROS Message Types and rosmsg show means messages are typed and can nest other types. use rosmsg show to inspect fields and plan publishers/subscribers correctly.. In practical terms, understanding typed messages and inspecting their structure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Message Types
Core idea

Typed messages and nesting

Messages define the fields you can read and write. Many message types nest other message types, so inspect structures before use.

Common types
  • std_msgs/String — text data
  • std_msgs/Int64 — integer numbers
  • geometry_msgs/Twist — linear and angular Vector3s
  • sensor_msgs/LaserScan — LiDAR ranges with angles
Inspecting messages
Command
rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist
Output shows linear and angular Vector3 fields with x, y, z components.
Example interpretation
For a planar robot use linear.x for forward velocity and angular.z for yaw rate; other axes are ignored in 2D contexts.

screens.title: Python Publisher Example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a typical Python publisher. The node initializes with rospy. init_node and creates a Publisher that advertises a topic and message type. The queue_size controls internal buffering when subscribers cannot keep up. Using rospy. Rate lets you publish at a stable frequency while accounting for loop work time. A concrete example node publishes a String message at two Hertz with a message body saying "Hello from the Robot News Radio." When the node publishes, pub. publish places the message into the outgoing buffer; sending is asynchronous. Remember to check rospy. is_shutdown in the loop so the node exits cleanly when ROS is shutting down. A common confusion is using time. sleep instead of rospy. Rate — time. sleep doesn't integrate with ROS shutdown signaling and can cause sluggish shutdowns. Practice: run the example, then open another terminal and run rostopic echo to confirm messages arrive and rostopic hz to confirm the 2 Hz rate. Takeaway: rospy. Rate and queue_size are simple but powerful controls for timing and buffering. How would you modify the node to publish integers at 1 Hz instead?

keyIdea.text: Use rospy.Publisher, rospy.Rate, and rospy.is_shutdown. queue_size controls buffering for slow subscribers.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Python Publisher
Example code
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import String

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('robot_news_radio', anonymous=True)
  pub = rospy.Publisher('/robot_news', String, queue_size=10)
  rate = rospy.Rate(2)  # 2 Hz

  while not rospy.is_shutdown():
    msg = String()
    msg.data = "Hello from the Robot News Radio!"
    pub.publish(msg)
    rospy.loginfo("Published: %s", msg.data)
    rate.sleep()
Key points
  • init_node sets up the node and name.
  • Publisher(topic, Type, queue_size) creates the publisher object.
  • rospy.Rate maintains consistent frequency and cooperates with shutdown handling.
Practice & verification
Try this
Run the node, then run rostopic echo /robot_news to see messages and rostopic hz /robot_news to check rate.
Pro tip
Use queue_size=1 for time-sensitive sensor streams to avoid processing stale data.
Common mistake
Using time.sleep breaks cooperative shutdown handling; prefer rospy.Rate for loops.

screens.title: C++ Publisher Example
screens.narratorSegment: C++ publishers follow a similar pattern to Python but use typed templates and compile-time linking. You initialize with ros::init and create a NodeHandle. Advertise a publisher using nh. advertise with the message type as a template parameter and a queue size. The node then enters a loop that runs while ros::ok and publishes messages with pub. publish. For example, a C++ publisher can send a std_msgs::String with the same greeting at two Hertz. A concrete example: run the compiled executable and watch ROS_INFO log messages that confirm publishing. Contrast with Python: C++ requires building into an executable and uses template types, whereas Python passes class objects at runtime. A frequent misconception is expecting identical tooling behavior — C++ may require recompilation after changes, while Python scripts run immediately. Why it matters: C++ is often used for performance-sensitive nodes, and knowing how to build and test publishers is essential. Takeaway: learn both language idioms so you can pick the right tool for the node's performance and development needs. What node in your system might benefit from a C++ implementation? content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › C++ Publisher
Example code
#include <ros/ros.h>
#include <std_msgs/String.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  ros::init(argc, argv, "robot_news_radio");
  ros::NodeHandle nh;
  ros::Publisher pub = nh.advertise<std_msgs::String>("/robot_news", 10);
  ros::Rate rate(2);  // 2 Hz

  while (ros::ok()) {
    std_msgs::String msg;
    msg.data = "Hello from the Robot News Radio!";
    pub.publish(msg);
    ROS_INFO("Published: %s", msg.data.c_str());
    rate.sleep();
  }

  return 0;
}
Key differences vs Python
  • Template-based advertise<T> syntax.
  • ros::ok mirrors rospy.is_shutdown semantics.
  • Requires building into an executable before running.
Build & test
Build steps
Add the node to CMakeLists, run catkin_make or colcon build, then run the executable with rosrun or roslaunch.
Pro tip
Use ROS logging to confirm publishing and compare timestamps when verifying rates across languages.

screens.title: Inspecting and Debugging Topics with rostopic
screens.narratorSegment: The rostopic command-line suite is indispensable for debugging topic-based systems. Use rostopic list to see active topics and rostopic info topic_name to learn which nodes publish or subscribe. rostopic echo topic_name prints message contents in real time, letting you confirm fields and values. To measure frequency, use rostopic hz topic_name, which shows the publishing rate; rostopic bw measures bandwidth. You can publish manually using rostopic pub for quick tests — for a one-off message use -1, or publish at a rate with -r. A concrete debugging workflow: if your robot doesn't move, run rostopic echo /cmd_vel to check for velocity messages, then rostopic hz /cmd_vel to confirm the rate. If messages exist but are old or missing fields, run rosmsg show on the message type to verify structure. A common mistake is relying only on visualization tools and not checking queue sizes. Also, rostopic pub can help inject test commands to isolate whether the issue is with the publisher or the subscriber. Takeaway: master a small set of rostopic commands and you'll diagnose most topic problems quickly. Which command will you use first when a topic seems silent?

screens.title: Queue Size and Message Buffering
screens.narratorSegment: queue_size is the publisher-side buffer limit that controls how many outgoing messages are stored when a subscriber cannot keep up. If the publisher generates messages faster than the subscriber can process, messages accumulate up to queue_size and older messages are dropped as new ones arrive. For time-sensitive streams like camera frames, small queues are preferable because processing old frames is often useless; in that case use queue_size of one so the subscriber sees the most recent data. For command logs or events where every message matters, choose a larger queue_size or consider a different communication primitive like services or actions. A concrete example: a camera publishes at 30 Hz while a processing node handles 5 Hz; with queue_size=10 the subscriber keeps the last ten frames and discards older ones, which might still be stale. A common misconception is thinking queue_size protects against network loss — it only controls in-process buffering. Takeaway: set queue_size based on whether you need latest-state freshness or full delivery. Consider what happens when multiple subscribers connect and the buffer fills — which policy serves your use case best?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Hands-on Activity

Step-by-step lab

Python: number_publisher.py
#!/usr/bin/env python3
import rospy
from std_msgs.msg import Int64

if __name__ == '__main__':
  rospy.init_node('number_publisher')
  pub = rospy.Publisher('/number', Int64, queue_size=10)
  rate = rospy.Rate(1)
  i = 1
  while not rospy.is_shutdown():
    msg = Int64()
    msg.data = i
    pub.publish(msg)
    i += 1
    rate.sleep()
C++: twist_publisher.cpp
// Build and run this node after adding to CMakeLists
#include <ros/ros.h>
#include <geometry_msgs/Twist.h>

int main(int argc, char** argv) {
  ros::init(argc, argv, "twist_publisher");
  ros::NodeHandle nh;
  ros::Publisher pub = nh.advertise<geometry_msgs::Twist>("/cmd_vel", 10);
  ros::Rate rate(2);
  while (ros::ok()) {
    geometry_msgs::Twist t;
    t.linear.x = 0.5;
    t.angular.z = 0.1;
    pub.publish(t);
    rate.sleep();
  }
  return 0;
}
Verification steps
  1. Run both publishers.
  2. Use rostopic echo /number and rostopic echo /cmd_vel to view messages.
  3. Use rostopic hz to confirm 1 Hz and 2 Hz rates.
  4. Publish a manual Twist with linear.x = 2.0 and observe behavior.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Debugging Checklist
screens.narratorSegment: When topics don't behave as expected, a short checklist solves most problems. First, check topic names and namespaces — a missing leading slash or wrong namespace is a frequent cause. Second, verify there are active publishers using rostopic info. Third, confirm message types match between publisher and subscriber; a type mismatch prevents communication. Fourth, review queue_size and timing: if your subscriber is slow you may see dropped messages or stale data. Fifth, ensure your node checks rospy. is_shutdown or ros::ok to shut down cleanly; leftover processes can confuse debugging. A concrete debugging flow: run rostopic list, then rostopic info on the topic, then rosmsg show on the message type, then rostopic echo to observe content, and finally rostopic hz to measure rate. A common misconception is assuming a topic with the right name implies matching types; always confirm type alignment. Takeaway: use a methodical checklist to isolate whether the problem is naming, type mismatch, buffering, or logic in the publisher/subscriber. screens.title: Assessment Idea and Scalability Discussion
screens.narratorSegment: Assessment: imagine a camera publishes images at 30 Hz to /camera/image_raw and an image processing node can only handle 5 images per second. What happens to the unprocessed images and how does queue_size affect this? The correct explanation is that unprocessed images accumulate in the subscriber's incoming buffer until the buffer fills; once full, older messages are dropped and the subscriber keeps the newest ones up to queue_size. If the subscriber uses a small queue, it processes mostly fresh frames; a large queue stores more history but increases staleness. This question tests understanding of buffering and data semantics. Now consider scalability: publish-subscribe is more scalable than point-to-point because a sensor publishes once and many algorithms subscribe without the sensor maintaining separate connections for each consumer. If there were N sensors and M algorithms, point-to-point would require O(N×M) connections; publish-subscribe reduces the active connection count to O(N+M) by centralizing discovery and allowing direct publisher-subscriber links. A common misconception is thinking discovery equals forwarding — it does not. Takeaway: choose publish-subscribe for many-to-many data flows and ensure buffer sizing matches your data needs.

fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how ROS nodes talk to each other using topics and publishers. We'll use the publish-subscribe model: a node publishes typed messages to a named topic and any number of subscribers can receive them. You will see why this decoupled approach scales for multiple sensors and algorithms, how the ROS Master helps nodes discover each other, and why messages flow directly between publishers and subscribers after discovery. We'll walk through message types and how to inspect them, then build publishers in Python and C++ that publish at fixed rates. I'll show command-line tools you can use to inspect topics, echo messages, measure rate, and even publish manually from a terminal. You will practice a small hands-on activity: a Python integer publisher and a C++ twist publisher, then verify behavior with rostopic. As you go, pay attention to the queue_size parameter and how buffering influences stale data. By the end you should be comfortable creating a simple publisher, checking message formats, and debugging common topic issues. What piece of sensor data from your robot would you publish as a topic?

These objectives map to practical skills you will use in ROS development. First, you will explain the publish-subscribe pattern and how topics implement it — that means describing one-to-many asynchronous messaging and the role of the ROS Master. Second, you will write a Python publisher that sends typed messages at a fixed rate and know why rospy. Rate and rospy. is_shutdown exist. Third, you will write an equivalent C++ publisher, compile it, and recognize the differences in A P I style and build process. Fourth, you will use rostopic and rosmsg tools to inspect, echo, measure rate, and publish messages from the terminal. Each objective pairs conceptual understanding with a hands-on task so you can prove the competency in a real ROS environment. For example, after the Python objective you'll be able to create a node that publishes integers at one Hertz and verify the numbers on the terminal. Keep in mind a common misconception: understanding code syntax is different from understanding how topics are discovered and how buffering affects data delivery. These objectives ensure you practice both sides.

This second objectives slide focuses on how to verify each skill. For publish-subscribe, verification is observing multiple subscribers receiving the same published message and explaining the Master's discovery process. For Python and C++ publishers, verification is running nodes that publish at a fixed rate and using rostopic hz to confirm the frequency. For message types and rosmsg, verification is running rosmsg show and interpreting the field types, such as geometry_msgs/Twist containing linear and angular Vector3 fields. For CLI tools, verification is using rostopic echo to view live messages and rostopic pub to inject test messages. A practical tip: when you validate a publisher, also validate clean shutdown behavior — the node should stop publishing when the system shuts down. A common misconception is assuming the Master forwards messages; instead, it only facilitates discovery. These verification steps ensure you can both explain concepts and demonstrate them in a live ROS setup.

Publish-subscribe is a messaging model where senders and receivers are decoupled. A publisher posts typed messages to a named topic without knowing who will read them; subscribers register interest in that topic and receive messages as they arrive. In ROS this model is asynchronous and one-to-many: one publisher can feed many subscribers, and subscribers can come and go without changing the publisher code. A concrete example: a laser scanner node publishes sensor_msgs/LaserScan to /laser/scan and a mapping node plus an obstacle detector can both subscribe independently. A common misconception is thinking the ROS Master forwards messages; it does not. The Master only helps nodes discover each other. After discovery each subscriber opens a direct TCP connection to each publisher so messages flow efficiently without the Master in the data path. Why it matters: this makes systems scalable and low-latency when many nodes need the same data. One pitfall to watch for is assuming message delivery is guaranteed; ROS topics are best-effort. Takeaway: design data flows so subscribers tolerate dropped or delayed messages, and choose queue sizes consciously to balance latency and loss. What sensor stream in your system should be best-effort and which needs guaranteed delivery?

A topic is a named bus for exchanging messages. Names look like paths: for example /robot/cmd_vel or /camera/image_raw. The leading slash denotes a global name; names without a leading slash are relative to the node's namespace. This lets you run multiple robots with identical node code by placing each instance in a different namespace such as /robot1 and /robot2. Topic names follow a filesystem-like hierarchy, so /robot1/cmd_vel and /robot2/cmd_vel are distinct. A concrete example: if you launch two teleop nodes under different namespaces, each teleop publishes to its namespace's /cmd_vel and the appropriate robot will receive commands. A common mistake is forgetting the leading slash and being surprised that topics don't match between nodes. Another misconception is thinking topic names are arbitrary strings; they must conform to ROS naming rules and avoid illegal characters. Why it matters: correct naming is essential when wiring a system with many nodes and when reusing code across multiple robots. Takeaway: choose consistent namespaces and be deliberate about global versus relative topic names. Which naming strategy would you use for two identical wheeled robots operating in the same network?

ROS messages are typed data structures defined in. msg files and compiled into language-specific classes. Standard messages include std_msgs/String for plain text, std_msgs/Int64 for integers, geometry_msgs/Twist for velocity commands, and sensor_msgs/Image for camera data. Knowing a message structure is crucial: it tells you which fields to set and what to expect when subscribing. Use rosmsg show followed by the message type to display the fields and nested types. For example, rosmsg show geometry_msgs/Twist reveals two Vector3 fields named linear and angular, each with x, y, and z components. A concrete example: for a mobile robot on a plane you typically use linear. x for forward speed and angular. z for rotation rate. A common confusion is assuming Twist has only scalar fields; instead it nests Vector3 structures. Why it matters: choosing the right message type avoids unnecessary conversions and ensures interoperability between nodes. Try rosmsg show on sensor_msgs/LaserScan to see how ranges and angle metadata are organized. Takeaway: always inspect message definitions before publishing or subscribing so you set and read the correct fields. In practical terms, understanding typed messages and inspecting their structure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When topics don't behave as expected, a short checklist solves most problems. First, check topic names and namespaces — a missing leading slash or wrong namespace is a frequent cause. Second, verify there are active publishers using rostopic info. Third, confirm message types match between publisher and subscriber; a type mismatch prevents communication. Fourth, review queue_size and timing: if your subscriber is slow you may see dropped messages or stale data. Fifth, ensure your node checks rospy. is_shutdown or ros::ok to shut down cleanly; leftover processes can confuse debugging. Assessment: imagine a camera publishes images at 30 Hz to /camera/image_raw and an image processing node can only handle 5 images per second. What happens to the unprocessed images and how does queue_size affect this? The correct explanation is that unprocessed images accumulate in the subscriber's incoming buffer until the buffer fills; once full, older messages are dropped and the subscriber keeps the newest ones up to queue_size. If the subscriber uses a small queue, it processes mostly fresh frames; a large queue stores more history but increases staleness. This question tests understanding of buffering and data semantics. Now consider scalability: publish-subscribe is more scalable than point-to-point because a sensor publishes once and many algorithms subscribe without the sensor maintaining separate connections for each consumer. If there were N sensors and M algorithms, point-to-point would require O(N×M) connections; publish-subscribe reduces the active connection count to O(N+M) by centralizing discovery and allowing direct publisher-subscriber links. A common misconception is thinking discovery equals forwarding — it does not. Takeaway: choose publish-subscribe for many-to-many data flows and ensure buffer sizing matches your data needs.

Let's summarize the most important points. First, publish-subscribe is one-to-many and asynchronous; the Master only handles discovery and not message forwarding. Second, topics are named buses with hierarchical names and namespaces that let you reuse code across robots; be careful with leading slashes. Third, messages are typed structures; use rosmsg show to inspect fields such as geometry_msgs/Twist which contains linear and angular Vector3 fields. Remember these three ideas when designing or debugging your ROS system: discovery versus forwarding, consistent naming, and correct message structure.
